thread.title: Dividend Sensei's Portfolio Update 63: Why I'm Now In Recession Prep Mode

author: Dividend Sensei
title: Dividend Sensei's Portfolio Update 63: Why I'm Now In Recession Prep Mode
text:
(Source: imgflip )
Note that due to reader requests, I've decided to break up my weekly portfolio updates into three parts: commentary, economic update, and portfolio summary, stats, and watch lists. This is to avoid excessively long articles and maximize the utility to my readers.
This week's commentary looks at five important factors that will determine whether or not we're already in a bear market .
Due to a family obligation, there is no economic update this week.
Introduction First, let me be very clear that this is my personal portfolio tailored to my specific financial situation, risk profile, time horizon, and personality traits. I am not recommending anyone mirrors this portfolio. My situation is that I'm 32 but consider this portfolio an income-focused retirement one (though in a taxable account, so I can use modest amounts of margin).
I'm also working full-time (self-employed) and am thus able to continually add to this portfolio. I do not plan to actually tap the portfolio's income stream for 14-20 years when I plan to move my family (and help support my parents) to the promised land of my people (retired dividend investors): Coastal Florida.
What this portfolio can be used for is investing ideas; however, this portfolio includes high-, low-, as well as medium-risk stocks, so it's up to each individual to do their own individual research and decide which, if any, of my holdings, are right for you.
For a detailed explanation of my methodology, please read my introductory article to the EDDGE (Eternal Daily Dividend Growth Experiment) 4.0 portfolio. However, keep in mind that the portfolio is not static, and both it and the underlying investment strategy will evolve and adapt over time. This is because a changing world, new knowledge, and more experience will cause me to fine-tune it over coming years and decades to maximize my income and total returns.
Also, note that this is currently a very sector concentrated portfolio. That's because I received my professional training working at The Motley Fool's energy desk, specializing in midstream MLPs (and also lots of renewable energy yieldCos). Thus, my comfort with these high-yield and very fast-growing industries. Since moving to Seeking Alpha (and becoming an analyst for Simply Safe Dividends), I've branched out into covering all industries. I now look at about 200 companies per year in detail. I spent most of the first year building out full positions in deeply undervalued midstream stocks and am now diversifying into other sectors (during each market downturn).
The bottom line is that researching dividend stocks is both my greatest passion and my profession. Thus, you should only use these updates as sources of ideas but not mirror them exactly unless your risk profile/time horizon/goals very closely match my own.
Why I'm Now In Recession Prep Mode... Because I've been using margin during the last two corrections to buy my highest conviction buys, I need to be extra conservative with my risk management protocols. This is because I want to maximize my chances of having little to no margin by the time the next bear market begins (preferably have some cash stored up). To achieve that I closely track the state of the economy each week . That's via seven separate models, most of which are themselves meta-analyses of leading economic indicators.
Since 82% of bear markets since WWII have occurred during recessions, the most important part of my macro analysis is based on the most proven recession predictor ever discovered, the yield curve. According to a March 2018 report from the San Francisco Fed, an inverted yield curve has " correctly signaled all nine recessions since 1955 and had only one false positive, in the mid-1960s, when an inversion was followed by an economic slowdown but not an official recession."
On December 3rd, the first of the yield curves (there are actually dozens of them) inverted for the first time since 2007. That was the 5y-3y curve, which over the last 40 years has never inverted (and stayed inverted) without the most famous curve (10y-2y) inverting soon after (within a few months). Thus the 5y-3y curve is a warning curve that my recession preparation protocol has been using as an early warning sign to start preparing for the next bear market. Note that on December 4th the 5y-2y curve also inverted and both curves have remained negative ever since.
However, as Guggenheim Partners CIO Scott Minerd points out, a yield curve inversion is not by itself a prediction of recession.
(Source: Jeff Miller )
And given that the curves that have inverted so far are merely the 5y-3y and 5y-2y (warning curves) which are not what financial institutions care about, we have to confirm with both the important curves and economic data that a recession is indeed becoming more like. That's because the reason the yield curve is a good recession predictor is that banks use it to determine lending policy.
Here's what the Dallas Fed's October 2018 bank survey found .
Banks were also asked how their lending policies would potentially change in response to a hypothetical moderate inversion of the (10y-3m) yield curve prevailing over the next year. Significant shares of banks indicated that they would tighten their standards or price terms across every major loan category if the yield curve were to invert ...Those banks that indicated they would tighten their lending policies because of an inversion of the yield curve were asked to provide reasons for their response. Major shares of banks indicated that their bank would interpret this scenario as signaling a less favorable or more uncertain economic outlook and as likely being followed by a deterioration in the quality of their existing loan portfolio . In addition, major shares of banks reported lending would become less profitable and their bank's risk tolerance would decrease in this scenario . " - Dallas Federal Reserve Bank Survey (emphasis added)
You'll note that American banks plan to use the 10y-3m curve as a warning sign to cut back on lending, especially to subprime borrowers. Since consumer spending is 65% to 70% of the US economy this shows that the yield curve is largely a self-fulfilling prophecy. Banks (and some other industries) believe that an inversion signals a recession is coming, so thus pullback on investment that causes the very recession they were expecting.
(Source: San Francisco Federal Reserve)
The reason the 10y-3M curve is what banks look at is that according to an August 2018 study by the San Fran Fed when it comes to predicting recessions, " The best summary measure is the spread between the ten-year and three-month yields. " This is because while warning curves are useful, for a yield curve to have strong recession predicting power requires a large enough duration gap. This is why warning curves like the 5y-3y don't by themselves indicate a recession is coming.
As of December 7th, here's where the four most accurate yield-curves sat :
10y-3m: 0.45% 10y-1y: 0.17% 10y-2y: 0.13% 30y-2y: 0.42% Note that a low yield curve is meaningless. Yield curves are all or none. Only if they are negative does the recession clock start ticking. The four most important curves are all still positive, with the 10y-3m, the most accurate recession predictor of all, being the most positive.
Since peaking in April 2010, the 10y-3m curve has been flattening at 3.2 basis points per month, indicating that it's now about 15 months away from inversion.
This means that my best estimate of when the next recession is likely to start is 24 to 31 months away (based on the latest bond market data). That would put the recession start date between December 2020 and June 2021.
Of course, as Scott Minerd says, the yield curve is merely one tool among many to track recession risk. To confirm that the economy is actually slowing and experiencing weaker fundamentals we need to use other tools and models.
(Source: Atlanta Federal Reserve)
(Source: New York Federal Reserve)
I use both the Atlanta and New York Fed models that estimate GDP growth based on economic updates, and both models are now calling for 2.4% GDP growth this quarter. That also agrees with the economist consensus which is 2.6% and has been trending down for months.
With US economic growth estimates to be 3.1% this year and 2.5% next year, 2.4% growth in Q4 might indicate that economic growth slows more than expected in 2019. For further confirmation, I turn to David Rice's BaR economic grid analysis.
(Source: David Rice)
David Rice (aka Economic PI) BaR economic grid analysis is an economic tracking model which uses 19 leading indicators that have accurately signaled the last four recessions. It analyzes how much above or below an indicator is relative to its historical norm, and how quickly the indicator is increasing or decreasing (thus baseline and rate of change or BaR).
Two weeks ago 16 of 19 indicators were pointing to continued economic growth with just three in the decline quadrant. Last week four more indicators started pointing to a declining economy. But since the number of indicators in any quadrant can be volatile from week to week, it's important to look at short-term (three month) and long-term (12 month) trends as well.
(Source: David Rice)
The good news is that most of the trends are still positive. The bad news is that more and more trends are turning negative and the leading indicators themselves are now below the overall mean of coordinates or MOC. The MOC is what I use as the best gauge for the overall fundamental health of the economy (based on how high it is above baseline).
(Source: David Rice)
As you can see, the three month average for MoC has been generally trending higher throughout the economic expansion. It now appears we have peaked and are set to start falling. Based on the last four recessions David concludes that when economic growth peaks the next recession begins about two years later. That agrees with the assessment of Blackstone's ( BX ) Byron Wien ( no recession until 2021 at the earliest ) as well as Deutsche Bank's latest economic forecast (no recession likely until 2022). That also happens to agree with my personal best estimate for a future recession based on the trend in the 10y-3M yield curve.
Now I have to point out that all this analysis merely indicates is that the US economy is likely to slow in 2019 and beyond. No official recession clock has yet started ticking. The reason why I'm personally in recession prep mode is that my goal is to pay off all margin before the market actually peaks, which Merrill Lynch's quant model says is most likely to occur around July 2020 . That also agrees with my personal assessment of the most likely start date for the next bear market (Dec 2019 to August 2020). That's based on the historical time lag between various yield curve inversions and when the stock market peaks (and a bear market begins).
But while that analysis might send me into defensive mode, it doesn't necessarily mean that's the right call for most of my readers, especially since most people appropriately don't use margin (it amplifies emotions which are historically the #1 thing that causes investor underperformance).
...But That Doesn't Necessarily Mean You Should Be It's very important to point out that while yield curves are highly accurate at predicting recessions (90% accuracy with a lead time of six to 24 months since 1955) they are less useful for predicting bear markets.
For example, the 10y-2y yield curve inversion usually means that stocks peak 19 months later, after rising 21% more. But looking at another important curve, the 10y-1y, we see that sometimes the market actually peaks before a yield curve inversion.
This is how I came to my estimate for the most likely start date for the next bear market of eight months to 19 months following an inversion of one of the important curves (which has not yet happened). But this is merely a probabilistic estimate based on historical averages. Due to the wide margin of error for such an analysis, and my personal situation and goals (margin free by the most likely next market top) I have to err on the side of caution and start my recession preparation protocol as soon as the earliest warning sign triggers. In this case that would be the 5y-3y warning curve inversion with confirmation of slowing economic fundamentals.
However, the fact remains that most of the time the market does surprisingly well after an inversion (22% median climb to the ultimate bull market top). And the year prior to a recession is also typically a positive one for stocks.
S&P 500 Before, During And After Recessions
(Source: Ben Carlson, Wealth Of Common Sense)
Heck in four of the last nine recession start years the market was actually up, by as much as 18.3%. This shows the importance of not timing the market by selling stocks in anticipation of a recession (which is always purely a probabilistic risk, not a guarantee).
This is why you'll note that my recession preparation protocol doesn't actually involve selling any stocks. This is because I have strong confidence in the recession-resistant cash flows of what I own, which makes dividend cuts (my chief concern) unlikely even during an economic downturn. And my average holding is 33% undervalued according to dividend yield theory, likely indicating that I have far less downside risk than the market in general. That has been confirmed thus far in this correction where my beta has been about 0.65. Combined with my high savings rate (which should allow me to pay off all margin by the end of 2019), I would be unlikely to face a margin call unless the market fell an additional 60% to 70% (I'm about 50% from a margin call myself). That would equate to a 70% to 80% market crash within a year, which is something that has literally never happened in US history (not even during the Great Depression where a 90% peak decline took two years to occur). Thus such a doomsday scenario is highly unlikely given the current economic and earnings fundamentals, market valuations, and the specific risk profile facing Wall Street specifically involving the trade war and Fed risk. What do I mean by that? Well simply that the more the market drops the more likely the Fed is to adopt a dovish stance including potentially just one more (or even no) more rate hikes. And what about the Trade war?
(Source: Trapping Value )
According to CNBC President Trump is very worried that the trade war might cause a bear market. For a man who considers the market a confirmation of his economic policies (to the point where he mentioned the strong rally during his last State of The Union), a bear market is very worrisome. The optics alone, of having the longest bull market in US history killed off by a trade war he chose to start (against the strong advice of most businessmen, economists, and advisors) would be terrible optics. Combined with a much weaker economy (and a possible recession by election day 2020), that could doom Trump's hopes of re-election. Thus the more stocks fall, the more likely Trump is to accept any trade deal China offers that even comes close to meeting his initial goals. And given that both Trump and economic advisory Larry Kudlow says that negotiations are "extremely promising" and " going very well " that makes it likely that Trump will strike a deal (likely by February if not sooner) and declare victory in his typically bombastic style (aka "the greatest trade deal ever made").
The bottom line is that while my specific situation and risk management rules have forced me to stop buying and become more defensive, it's not necessarily the right call for most of my readers. That's especially true given that the current correction has created an incredible number of high-quality, deeply undervalued dividend growth stocks. For example today there are 22 great stocks worth buying off my five watchlists.
The Best Dividend Growth Stocks You Can Buy Today This group of 20 dividend growth blue chips represents what I consider the best stocks you can buy today. They are presented in four categories, sorted by most undervalued (based on dividend yield theory using a 5-year average yield).
High yield (4+% yield) Fast dividend growth Dividend Aristocrats Monthly dividend stocks Note there may be some overlap between these groups. To help with further research, I've linked to my articles for each recommendation (those not behind a paywall).
The goal is to allow readers to know what are the best low-risk dividend growth stocks to buy at any given time. You can think of these as my "highest-conviction" recommendations for conservative income investors. Note these are not meant to represent a diversified or complete portfolio, but merely highlight the best opportunities for low-risk income investors available in the market today.
The valuations are determined by dividend yield theory, which Investment Quality Trends, or IQT, has proven works well for dividend stocks since 1966, generating market-crushing long-term returns with far less volatility.
(Source: Investment Quality Trends )
That's because, for stable business income stocks, yields tend to mean-revert over time, meaning cycle around a relatively fixed value approximating fair value. If you buy a dividend stock when the yield is far above its historical average, then you'll likely outperform when its valuation returns to its normal level over time.
For the purposes of these valuation-adjusted total return potentials, I use the Gordon Dividend Growth Model or GDGM. Since 1956, this has proven relatively accurate at modeling long-term total returns via the formula: Yield + dividend growth. That's because, assuming no change in valuation, a stable business model (doesn't change much over time) and a constant payout ratio, dividend growth tracks cash flow growth.
The valuation adjustment assumes that a stock's yield will revert to its historical norm within 10 years (over that time period, stock prices are purely a function of fundamentals). Thus, these valuation total return models are based on the formula: Yield + projected 10-year dividend growth (analyst consensus, confirmed by historical growth rate) + 10-year yield reversion return boost.
For example, if a stock with a historical average yield of 2% is trading at 3%, then the yield is 50% above its historical yield. This implies the stock is (3% current yield - 2% historical yield)/3% current yield = 33% undervalued. If the stock mean-reverts over 10 years, then this means the price will rise by 50% over 10 years just to correct the undervaluation.
That represents a 4.1% annual total return just from valuation mean regression. If the stock grows its cash flow (and dividend) at 10% over this time, then the total return one would expect from this stock would be 3% yield + 10% dividend (and FCF/share) growth + 4.1% valuation boost = 17.1%.

Buys/Sells This Week None: recession prep mode means not buying stocks even during a correction Tentative Plan For The Upcoming Week/Weeks As long as my recession prep protocols remain in effect, meaning the 5y-3y warning curve remains inverted and economic indicators continue to trend lower, I won't be buying any stocks no matter how low they fall.
Obviously given the incredible number of bargains currently on offer I'm hoping that factors improve so I can add a starting position in Broadcom, which is hands down the best high-yield tech blue-chip you can buy today. But in order to maintain discipline and err on the side of caution, I don't expect any purchases for the foreseeable future, possibly including all of 2019.
As a result, I will no longer be doing weekly portfolio updates, but switch to a quarterly update schedule. That's because with no changes to the portfolio the large amount of portfolio stats I present won't be changing over time. But due to my heavy exposure to midstream stocks (most who hike distributions on a quarterly basis), a quarterly update will be appropriate.
I'll be switching to a weekly "best stocks you can buy today" article based on my watchlists. I'll also be starting a tracking portfolio where once a month I buy $500 of each of the top 5 stocks in each watchlist (other than the monthly payers) and the bear market buy list. I'll be tracking that portfolio (but in a highly abbreviated form) each week in those future updates.
This will give investors an idea of how well my overall investing approach works in all manner of economic and market conditions when applied to only low-risk blue-chip stocks (like the ones that I recommend for most of my readers).

The long-term goal is to diversify to the point where no single position accounts for more than 5% of my income. However, it will take several years to diversify the portfolio to that point. Fortunately, all my biggest income producers have safe dividends/distributions.
(Source: Morningstar)
The portfolio has become far more diversified by stock style, especially compared to the early days, when it was pretty much 100% small-cap value. That being said, I'm fundamentally a value-focused investor, and so, will always be overweight in that investing style. Meanwhile, my heavy US exposure is due to the heavy concentration of hard assets, most notably MLPs.
(Source: Morningstar)
My portfolio is very concentrated in energy because that's where the best overall opportunities are in terms of safe yield, fast payout growth, and valuation. But now that my midstream MLP buildout is complete (full positions in all my highest-conviction buys), I'll be working on diversifying into more ultra-value REITs, utilities (yieldCos), and any other great opportunities I find. I've come down from about 70% hard assets to just 50%, thanks to all the diversification I was able to do during this correction.
Sector Concentration I've managed to diversify down from 59% energy to just 39% thanks to buying other sectors so aggressively during this correction.
(Source: Simply Safe Dividends) note consumer discretionary is Amazon, so 10% of my portfolio is actually in technology stocks, which is now tied for my 4th largest sector.
(Source: Morningstar)
The benefit of my currently concentrated portfolio is that I enjoy far better fundamental stats than the S&P 500. That includes lower valuation, much higher yield, and superior long-term growth potential. I'm also running a mostly midcap portfolio, with above-average profitability, and that should generate market-beating long-term returns.
In the future, I plan to add more utilities to help build up the defensive side of my portfolio. The new utilities I'll be buying include:
Brookfield Renewable Partners ( BEP ) TerraForm Power ( TERP ) Atlantica Yield ( AY ) In the meantime, my limit orders are focused on the most undervalued, fast-growing blue chips I know of, mostly industrial, pharma, and financial stocks.
(Source: Simply Safe Dividends)
Note that the 10-year dividend growth figures are artificially low because my tracking software doesn't average in anything that hasn't existed for those time periods. Some of my holdings have IPO-ed in the last five years, and so, the 1-year and 5-year growth rates are the most accurate. These figures are purely organic growth rates and assume no dividend reinvestment. The dividend declines during the Financial Crisis were due to three of the REITs, I own cutting their dividends (78 REITs did during the Great Recession). Fortunately, since then, the sector has deleveraged and enjoys the strongest sector balance sheet in history.
(Source: Hoya Capital Real Estate)
That means that, during the next recession, most REITs will NOT cut their payouts, especially the ones I own. The long-term goal is to maintain a 10+% organic income growth rate.

Even assuming no dividend reinvestment (I do that manually) and that I never sell anything I own (if growth slows and I find better opportunities), this portfolio would become an income powerhouse. And even if I were to not add to the portfolio at all with fresh savings within 20 years, I would have achieved my goal of financial independence.
Over the long term, my goal is about 5% portfolio yield, with about 10% long-term dividend growth over time. In order to maintain that, I may have to recycle some holdings when they no longer meet my needs.
For perspective, the S&P 500 yields 1.9%, and its 20-year median annual dividend growth rate has been 6.4% . So, the goal is about to triple the market's yield, with about 4% faster dividend growth. Since 1871, the S&P 500 has generated annual total returns of 9.2% . The market's historical inflation-adjusted total return has been 7.0%.
Even assuming no valuation multiple expansion (my deeply undervalued portfolio always remains so), this portfolio should easily be capable of about 15% un-levered total returns over time. Factoring in multiple expansion (which is already starting to happen for some of my stocks) and 25% leverage, the returns could be even greater, potentially north of 20% annualized net levered returns.
